claims.text: Corrosion protection of pre-exposure Q235 steel in an aggressive salt environment at room temperature is mainly caused by a coherent, adherent Fe3O4 scale.
A predominantly Fe3O4 scale forms in situ on Q235 steel during room-temperature salt exposure.
Heating salt-exposed Q235 steel to 700–900 °C transforms some or all of the Fe3O4 scale into Fe2O3 or other less protective oxides.
The high-temperature oxide products on Q235 steel are less coherent and less adherent than the room-temperature Fe3O4 scale.
Thermal stresses during high-temperature exposure promote oxide-scale spallation.
Room-temperature kinetics favor formation of a uniform and coherent protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
A dense, coherent oxide layer can hinder continued oxidation or corrosion.
High-temperature salt exposure causes rapid oxidation of Q235 steel.
High-temperature exposure increases oxide-scale porosity and reduces scale adhesion on Q235 steel.
Porosity and spallation expose the Q235 substrate to continued corrosive attack.
Oxide transformation and spallation cause greater corrosion degradation at 700–900 °C than at room temperature.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 coupons will exhibit significantly greater mass loss than room-temperature salt-exposed coupons.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 coupons will exhibit greater surface and microstructural damage than room-temperature controls.
XRD will show dominant magnetite after room-temperature exposure and hematite or mixed oxides after high-temperature exposure.
Microscopy will show more spallation and a less intact scale after high-temperature exposure.
The proposed mechanism requires an oxidizing, aggressive salt chemistry and enough exposure time for scale transformation.
The mechanism should not apply in inert or non-corrosive environments where oxygen availability or salt chemistry prevents stable oxide formation.
Changing chloride or sulfate content may prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.
Additional alloying elements or protective coatings can change oxide-scale formation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Minor alloying elements, impurities, salt composition, heating duration, and thermal cycling may alter oxide stability and the observed outcome.
